steps.title: A sea of electrons
steps.body: Metal atoms have only a few outer electrons and give them up easily. In a piece of metal, every atom releases its outer electrons into a shared pool. What is left is a **giant structure**: a regular lattice of **positive ions** surrounded by a **sea of delocalised electrons**. *Delocalised* means not tied to any one atom: free to move through the whole structure. The **electrostatic attraction** between the positive ions and the negative electrons is the metallic bond, and it is strong.

visuals.alt: Metallic structure: rows of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them

check.prompt: In metallic bonding, what is delocalised?
check.solution: The electrons move; the ions stay in place.
options: The outer electrons
The positive ions
The protons
The whole atoms

steps.title: Why metals conduct
steps.body:
Electricity is a flow of charge. The delocalised electrons can move through the metal, so metals **conduct electricity** as solids and as liquids. The same electrons carry thermal energy quickly from a hot part of the metal to a cold part, so metals **conduct heat** too.

Most metals have **high melting points** because the attraction between the ions and the electrons is strong throughout the structure and needs a lot of energy to overcome.

check.prompt: Which particles move when a metal conducts electricity?
check.solution: Unlike molten ionic compounds, where ions carry the charge, in a metal it is the electrons.
options: Delocalised electrons
Positive ions
Both ions and electrons
Neutrons

visuals.problem: Explain why aluminium is used for overhead power cables

steps.text: Aluminium has delocalised electrons that are free to move
They carry charge through the metal, so it conducts electricity
It is also light and does not corrode badly, which matters for long cables

steps.title: Why metals bend
steps.body: In a pure metal the ions are all the same size and pack in neat **layers**. Push hard enough and a layer **slides** over the one below. The delocalised electrons move with it and keep holding everything together, so the metal changes shape without breaking. That is why metals are **malleable** (can be hammered) and **ductile** (can be drawn into wires).

visuals.alt: Metallic structure: layers of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons

visuals.problem: Explain why copper can be drawn into wires

steps.text: Copper ions are the same size and arranged in layers
The layers can slide over each other
The delocalised electrons still attract the ions, so the structure holds together as it changes shape

check.prompt: Why does a pure metal not shatter when hit?
check.solution: Sliding layers plus electrons that keep bonding: both halves are needed.
options: The layers of ions slide and the delocalised electrons keep the structure bonded
The metallic bonds are weak, so they absorb the energy of the blow without breaking
The ions are far apart, so there is empty space for them to move into when hit
The electrons are fixed in place, so they hold the ions firmly in their positions

steps.title: Alloys: mixing in other atoms
steps.body:
Pure metals are often **too soft** to be useful. Pure iron bends; pure gold scratches. An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. The added atoms are a **different size**, so they **distort the regular layers**. Distorted layers cannot slide over each other easily, so alloys are **harder** than the pure metals they are made from.

- **Steel**: iron with a little carbon (and sometimes chromium, nickel).
- **Brass**: copper and zinc. **Bronze**: copper and tin.
- **18-carat gold**: 75% gold with silver and copper.

An alloy is still a metal: it keeps its delocalised electrons, so it still conducts and still has a metallic shine. Only the sliding of the layers has changed.

visuals.alt: Left: a pure metal with identical ions in regular layers that can slide. Right: an alloy where larger atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide.

visuals.problem: Why is brass harder than pure copper?

steps.text: Zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms
They distort the regular layers of ions
The layers cannot slide as easily, so brass is harder

check.prompt: Why is steel harder than pure iron?
options: Carbon atoms are a different size from iron atoms and distort the layers, so they cannot slide easily
Carbon forms strong covalent bonds with the iron atoms, which lock every layer firmly into place
Steel has more delocalised electrons than pure iron, so its metallic bonding is much stronger
Iron atoms grow bigger when carbon is added, so the layers are heavier and harder to move

steps.title: Your turn: property to explanation
steps.body:
For each property, name the feature of metallic bonding that explains it:

- **Conducts electricity**: delocalised electrons move and carry charge.
- **Conducts heat**: delocalised electrons carry thermal energy.
- **High melting point**: strong attraction between ions and delocalised electrons.
- **Malleable**: layers of ions slide, electrons keep the bonding.
- **Alloy is harder**: different sized atoms distort layers so they cannot slide.

check.prompt: Which feature of metallic bonding explains why a metal has a high melting point?
check.solution: Melting means overcoming the bonding; here that is the ion-to-electron attraction.

markScheme.description: Strong attraction between ions and electrons

options: The strong electrostatic attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
The regular layers of positive ions, which are difficult to pull apart from each other
The different sizes of the ions, which stop the layers from sliding when heated
The strong covalent bonds between the metal atoms, which need a lot of energy to break

visuals.problem: Why is gold jewellery made from an alloy, not pure gold?

steps.text: Pure gold: identical ions in regular layers that slide easily, so it is soft
Add silver and copper: different sized atoms distort the layers
Layers cannot slide as easily, so the alloy is harder and keeps its shape

steps.title: Grade 9: use the group number
steps.body:
A metal in Group 1 gives one electron per atom to the sea; Group 2 gives two; Group 3 (aluminium) gives three. More delocalised electrons and a higher ion charge mean a **stronger** attraction, so a higher melting point. Within a group of similar metals it usually means better conduction too, though other things matter as well: copper gives up only one electron per atom and is still the best everyday conductor. That is why magnesium melts at 650 °C and sodium at 98 °C.

The other grade 9 move is to spot the difference between metallic and ionic conduction: in a **metal**, electrons move and it conducts as a solid; in an **ionic compound**, ions move, so it conducts only when molten or dissolved.

visuals.problem: Why does aluminium conduct better than sodium?

steps.text: Aluminium is in Group 3: three delocalised electrons per atom
Sodium is in Group 1: one per atom
More charge carriers, so aluminium conducts better

check.prompt: Calcium is in Group 2 and potassium in Group 1. Which will have the higher melting point, and why?
check.solution: Higher charge and more delocalised electrons mean stronger metallic bonding.

markScheme.description: Calcium: 2+ ions and two electrons per atom

options: Calcium, because Ca²⁺ ions and two delocalised electrons per atom give a stronger attraction
Potassium, because it has more electrons in total, so its sea of electrons is larger
Calcium, because it forms covalent bonds between its atoms as well as metallic bonds
They will be the same, because both are metals and all metallic bonds are equally strong

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Metallic bonding: a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, held by strong electrostatic attraction.
- Delocalised electrons carry charge and thermal energy: metals conduct as solids.
- Layers of ions slide over each other: metals are malleable and ductile.
- Alloys: different sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide, making the alloy harder.
- Higher group number means more delocalised electrons and stronger bonding.

visuals.alt: Metallic structure: positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons

questions.prompt: Metallic bonding is best described as
questions.solution: Metal atoms lose their outer electrons into a shared pool: delocalised means free to move through the whole structure.
options: positive metal ions in a regular pattern with a sea of delocalised electrons
shared pairs of electrons between neighbouring metal atoms in a giant lattice
positive and negative metal ions attracted to each other in a regular pattern
metal molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces in a regular pattern

questions.solution: Only the delocalised electrons move. The ions stay in their places in the lattice.
options: Its delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the metal
Its positive ions are free to move and carry charge through the metal
It contains a small amount of water, which carries the charge through the metal
Its covalent bonds pass electrons from one copper atom to the next

questions.solution: Alloys are mixtures, not compounds. Brass is copper with zinc; steel is iron with carbon.

markScheme.description: Mixture of a metal with other elements

options: a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements
a compound formed when two metals react together
a pure metal that has been heated and cooled quickly
a metal that has been dissolved in water and dried

questions.prompt: Why can pure metals be bent and shaped?
questions.solution: Sliding layers is the key phrase, plus the electrons keep the bonding, so the metal does not break.
options: The layers of ions can slide over each other while the delocalised electrons keep holding the structure together
The ions are not bonded to each other at all, so they can be pushed into any shape without resistance
The metallic bonds break easily when a force is applied, then re-form when the force is removed
The ions are very small, so they can squeeze past each other when the metal is bent or hammered

questions.prompt: Why are alloys usually harder than pure metals?
questions.solution: Regular layers slide; distorted ones jam. That single idea explains why almost every metal you use is an alloy.

markScheme.description: Different sized atoms distort layers, layers cannot slide

options: The different sized atoms distort the regular layers, so they cannot slide over each other as easily
The added atoms form much stronger metallic bonds, so more force is needed to move the layers
The added atoms form covalent bonds with the metal atoms, which lock the layers firmly in place
The added atoms provide extra delocalised electrons, which pull the layers more tightly together

questions.prompt: Why do metals have high melting points?
questions.solution: Metallic bonding is a strong electrostatic attraction between ions and delocalised electrons throughout the structure.

markScheme.description: Strong attraction between ions and delocalised electrons

options: The electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons is strong and needs a lot of energy to overcome
The positive ions are large and heavy, so a lot of energy is needed to make them move apart from each other
The delocalised electrons are held very tightly by the nucleus of each atom, so a lot of energy is needed to free them
The atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds in a giant lattice, and many of these must be broken to melt the metal

questions.prompt: Explain why metals are good conductors of heat.
questions.solution: Same electrons, different job: charge for electricity, energy for heat.

criteria.text: The electrons are free to move through the structure
They carry thermal energy quickly from the hot part to the cold part

questions.modelAnswer: Metals contain delocalised electrons that are free to move throughout the structure. When one part is heated, these electrons gain energy and move quickly, transferring thermal energy through the metal.

questions.prompt: Steel is an alloy of iron and which non-metal?
questions.solution: Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon, sometimes with other metals added too.

questions.prompt: Gold used in jewellery is usually an alloy containing about 75% gold with silver and copper, rather than pure gold. Using ideas about structure and bonding, explain why.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Top answers explain both the softness of the pure metal and the mechanism by which the added atoms fix it.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about sliding layers in the pure metal and distorted layers in the alloy, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of sliding layers in the pure metal and distorted layers in the alloy with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of sliding layers in the pure metal and distorted layers in the alloy using the correct terms

criteria.text: Pure gold has a regular lattice of identical ions in layers
The layers slide over each other easily, so pure gold is soft and would scratch or bend
Silver and copper atoms are different sizes from gold atoms
So the layers cannot slide as easily and the alloy is harder
The alloy still contains delocalised electrons, so it keeps its metallic properties such as lustre and conduction

questions.modelAnswer: In pure gold the ions are all the same size and pack in regular layers. These layers can slide over each other easily, so pure gold is soft and jewellery made from it would scratch and bend. Adding silver and copper introduces atoms of different sizes into the lattice. They distort the regular layers, so the layers can no longer slide as easily, and the alloy is harder and more hard-wearing. The alloy still has delocalised electrons throughout, so it keeps the shine and conductivity of a metal.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares metallic and ionic bonding?
questions.solution: Both are strong electrostatic attractions. The difference is what is attracting what, which explains the difference in conduction.

markScheme.description: Both electrostatic; ions and electrons versus ions and ions

options: Both are electrostatic attractions: between positive ions and delocalised electrons in a metal, and between oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound
Metallic bonding is a type of covalent bonding, whereas ionic bonding is an electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Ionic compounds contain delocalised electrons that carry charge, whereas metals contain only fixed positive and negative ions
Metals conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, in exactly the same way as ionic compounds do

questions.prompt: Magnesium and sodium are both metals. Magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium and is a better conductor. Suggest why, using ideas about metallic bonding.
questions.solution: Uses group number to predict ion charge and number of delocalised electrons, then links both to properties.

markScheme.description: Two delocalised electrons per atom versus one

criteria.text: Magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions, sodium forms Na⁺ ions
Magnesium releases two delocalised electrons per atom, sodium only one
The attraction between the 2+ ions and the larger number of delocalised electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to melt magnesium
More delocalised electrons per atom means more charge carriers, so magnesium conducts better

questions.modelAnswer: Each magnesium atom loses two outer electrons to become Mg²⁺, while each sodium atom loses one to become Na⁺. So magnesium has ions with a higher charge and twice as many delocalised electrons per atom. The electrostatic attraction between the 2+ ions and the sea of electrons is stronger, so more energy is needed to break it and the melting point is higher. The extra delocalised electrons also mean more charge carriers, so magnesium conducts electricity better.

questions.prompt: A student says "alloys are harder because the bonds between the different atoms are stronger". Why is this wrong?
questions.solution: The examiner wants the layer-sliding explanation, not "stronger bonds".
options: Alloy hardness comes from different sized atoms distorting the layers so they cannot slide, not from stronger bonds
Alloys are not actually harder than pure metals; they are only more resistant to corrosion and easier to melt
Alloys have no metallic bonds, because the different atoms form covalent bonds with each other instead
The bonds in an alloy are weaker than in the pure metal, and weaker bonds make the layers harder to move

questions.prompt: Aluminium is in Group 3. How many delocalised electrons does each aluminium atom contribute to the metallic structure?
questions.skill: linking group number to metallic bonding
questions.solution: Group number gives the number of outer electrons, and a metal atom releases all of them into the sea of electrons.

questions.prompt: Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. Which statement must be true?
questions.skill: applying metallic bonding to an unusual metal
questions.solution: A low melting point means weaker metallic bonding, but mercury still has delocalised electrons and conducts, which is why it was used in thermometers and switches.

markScheme.description: Weaker metallic bonding, still delocalised electrons

options: The attraction between its ions and delocalised electrons is weaker than in most metals, so less energy is needed to overcome it
Mercury has no delocalised electrons, so there is no metallic bonding to hold its atoms in a fixed lattice
Mercury cannot really be a metal, because every true metal is a solid with a high melting point
Mercury atoms are held together by covalent bonds, which are much weaker than metallic bonds

examTechnique.body: Metallic bonding questions reward one precise sentence per property. Always name the particles: "positive ions" and "delocalised electrons". For alloys, the mark is for "different sized atoms distort the layers so they cannot slide", never for "stronger bonds".
examinerErrors: Saying metals conduct because "the ions move". In a solid metal only the electrons move.
Saying "free electrons" without "delocalised". Either is usually accepted, but delocalised is the specification word.
Describing metallic bonding as covalent or as "atoms sharing electrons".
Forgetting that malleability needs both halves: layers slide and the electrons keep the bonding.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the ions and the delocalised electrons, uses the group number to predict ion charge and electron count, explains both the softness of a pure metal and the hardness of its alloy through layers, and can contrast metallic with ionic conduction.
